summary: This document analyzes the security implications of using IPv6 fragmentation with Neighbor Discovery messages. It updates RFC 4861 to forbid the Fragment Header in all Neighbor Discovery messages, allowing simple countermeasures. It also discusses fragmentation with Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) and updates RFC 3971 with advice.

eli5.summary: Cutting neighbor-finding messages into pieces lets attackers sneak in. This says do not cut them up.

questions: are fragments allowed in ipv6 neighbor discovery
can ipv6 neighbor discovery messages be fragmented
why is ipv6 fragmentation a security risk
subtitle: Why IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages must not be fragmented.

tldr.problem: Attackers can hide Neighbor Discovery attacks by splitting packets into IPv6 fragments, which defeats filters such as RA-Guard and monitoring tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC forbids sending fragmented Neighbor Discovery messages and requires nodes to silently ignore those that arrive fragmented, with a softer rule for SEND Certification Path Advertisements.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 4861 and RFC 3971. Filtering and monitoring Neighbor Discovery becomes much simpler, at the cost of ignoring a rarely needed capability.

today: RFC 6980 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 4861 and RFC 3971.

sections.title: The Fragmentation Problem
sections.content:
The Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) of RFC 4861 is used by hosts and routers for functions such as router discovery, address autoconfiguration, address resolution and redirection. Attacks on it are described in RFC 3756. SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) addresses them but is hard to deploy, so other mitigations are common: access control lists in switches, layer-2 filtering such as RA-Guard (RFC 6105), monitoring tools and intrusion prevention systems.

Fragmentation undermines all of these. An attacker can split the attack packet so that a layer-2 device cannot find the information it needs in a single packet. The RFC says current RA-Guard implementations can be trivially evaded this way, and that monitoring tools which try to reassemble fragments end up in an arms race with the attacker.
sections.eli5: Guards check each note as it goes by. If a note is torn into pieces, no single piece looks bad, so the guards miss it.

sections.title: Traditional Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
The only plausible reason to fragment a traditional (non-SEND) Neighbor Discovery message is a Router Advertisement carrying a very large number of options, such as Prefix Information and Route Information options. That can be avoided by splitting the information into several Router Advertisements.

Doing so is also better for interoperability, because some implementations are known to silently ignore Router Advertisements that are fragmented. Avoiding fragmentation therefore simplifies and improves filtering and monitoring and prevents problems with implementations that do not support it.
sections.eli5: If you have too much to say, write two short notes instead of tearing one long note in half.

sections.title: SEND and Certification Paths
sections.content:
SEND packets carry more data, such as the Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA) option and the RSA signature option. For most SEND messages the answer is the same as for plain ND: split the information over several messages.

Certification Path Advertisement (CPA) messages are different, because the Certificate Option is much larger than other ND options. RFC 3971 reports CPA messages of 1050 to 1066 bytes on Ethernet, which could exceed the link MTU. Relying on fragmentation here opens SEND to attack. An attacker on the same broadcast domain could forge fragments that cause Fragment ID collisions, so that both the attack and the legitimate fragments are discarded. Authorization Delegation Discovery would then fail, and the host would either fall back to unsecured mode or reject the Router Advertisements, possibly leading to denial of service.
sections.eli5: The secure version of the note includes a big ID card that sometimes will not fit in one envelope. A trickster can mess with the pieces so the ID card never gets put back together.

sections.title: Rationale for Forbidding Fragmentation
sections.content:
The RFC gives three reasons. A significant number of implementations already silently drop fragmented ND messages, so fragmenting hurts interoperability. Such messages are unlikely to exist in practice, because exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1280 octets would take a large number of options. And any oversized message can be replaced by several smaller ones.

Forbidding fragmentation therefore normalizes existing behavior and sets every implementation's expectation to the lowest common denominator.
sections.eli5: Most neighbors already throw away torn notes, and nobody really needs to send one, so making it a rule costs almost nothing.

sections.title: The Specification
sections.content:
Nodes MUST NOT use IPv6 fragmentation to send Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement, Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Redirect or Certification Path Solicitation messages. They MUST silently ignore any of those that arrive in a packet with a Fragment Header.

Certification Path Advertisement is handled more gently: nodes SHOULD NOT fragment it and SHOULD normally process it if it arrives fragmented. SEND nodes SHOULD NOT use keys that would cause fragmented CPA messages.

This section formally updates RFC 4861 and gives advice that updates RFC 3971.
sections.eli5: Do not tear these notes, and throw away any torn ones you get. The one big ID card note is allowed to arrive in pieces, but try not to need that.

sections.title: Operational Advice and Message Sizes
sections.content:
If an operator sees Neighbor Discovery traffic being silently dropped, the cause may be fragmentation. The operator should check whether the sender can be told not to fragment ND messages, or whether the options carried can be reduced. The RFC notes that a fix may need a software upgrade.

Appendix A estimates CPA sizes. With 1024-bit keys the certificates are 864 to 888 bytes and the Ethernet packets 1050 to 1066 bytes. With the 2048-bit keys required by RFC 6494, packets range from 1127 to 1238 bytes, below the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1280 bytes. Larger keys, for example 4096 bits, might need a larger MTU to avoid fragmentation.
sections.eli5: If notes keep vanishing, check whether they are being torn up, and try shorter notes. The big ID card still fits in a normal envelope for now.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Fragment Header can be used to evade network monitoring tools and current RA-Guard implementations. Disallowing it in every Neighbor Discovery message except Certification Path Advertisement greatly simplifies both protecting local nodes and monitoring ND traffic.

Because SEND could still produce fragmented CPA messages, which an attacker can target with fragmentation-based attacks, the RFC says such use should be avoided as far as possible.
sections.eli5: With no torn notes allowed, guards can read every note whole. The only exception is the big ID card, which should be avoided where possible.
